title: Redwood Discovery - Aurora Logistics - Latency & Throughput
transcript:
Header: Recorded on 2026-05-05 14:00 PT | Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sam Lee (Aurora Head of ML), Priya Patel (Infra), Tom Raines (CTO), Jenna (PM)

Summary: Early discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput needs for Aurora's real-time routing features. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, streaming, concurrency and token/sec benchmarking. Next steps: provide SOC2/network docs, pricing for dedicated pilot, seed benchmark account and run token/sec tests.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Tom: yes, loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:07] Maya: cool, so quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood infra team, and Diego is our solutions engineer who will dig into latency and throughput.
[00:15] Diego: hi all, quick agenda, want to understand current stack, p95 targets, concurrency, and whether streaming is needed, then we'll talk deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private) and benchmarking approach.
[00:26] Sam: great, I'm Sam, lead ML. We run real-time route optimization, need sub-200ms p95 for short prompts (50-150 tokens) and scale to about 300 concurrent sessions during peaks.
[00:36] Priya: infra side, we currently run Kubernetes on GCP, private VPC, we have strict egress controls and KMS requirements for keys.
[00:44] Maya: perfect, that helps. quick clarify — when you say sub-200ms p95 is that including network egress back to your app or purely inference time?
[00:52] Sam: ideally end-to-end from request to first token, so includes transit inside cloud region but we can host near them.
[00:58] Diego: ok, so p95 end-to-end target ~200ms for 50–150 token prompts. For hosted Redwood API our typical p95 numbers on optimized open models are in the 80–180ms range for short inputs on accelerated instances, but depends on model size, quantization, and concurrency.
[01:15] Jenna: and we need streaming for partial tokens — the UI shows live updates.
[01:18] Diego: streaming supported, yes, with chunked responses. Important note: streaming adds some latency amortization quirks, we can typically deliver first token < p50, p95 for completion may be similar depending on model.
[01:32] Tom: what's the trade-off between hosted and dedicated for latency and cost?
[01:36] Maya: hosted is fastest to start — no infra setup, predictable latencies for low concurrency. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so better tail latency at scale and no noisy-neighbor variability; private (VPC/on-prem) is for data residency/compliance with slightly more ops overhead.
[01:49] Priya: we are highly security-sensitive, SOC2 and audit logs required, plus our keys must be in our KMS.
[01:55] Maya: we support SOC2 and SSO/SAML, and for Private we integrate customer KMS/HSM and provide audit logs. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[02:03] Sam: can you run KV cache — sorry I mean KV cache, does your runtime keep state across tokens to reduce compute?
[02:09] Diego: yes KV cache is supported to avoid re-computation on streaming and multi-turn; we also support prefix caching and automatic batching which helps token/sec throughput.
[02:18] Sam: cool. what throughput should we expect per GPU? we have a benchmark target of 1,500 tokens/sec sustained across the cluster.
[02:26] Diego: depends on model and quantization. For a quantized 7B variant on A100-like hardware, we typically see 200–400 tokens/sec per GPU for generation workloads, higher for shorter sequences; with batching we can push aggregate token/sec higher — dedicated pools scale linearly with reserved GPU count.
[02:40] Tom: that seems lower than our target, can batching and multiple GPUs meet our 1,500 tokens/sec?
[02:46] Diego: yes, if you reserve ~4–8 GPUs depending on model and prompt length you can hit sustained 1.5k tokens/sec, and with smart routing we can shard requests across dedicated nodes to keep p95 low.
[02:58] Priya: any examples of p95 under load? we want historic numbers not marketing.
[03:03] Diego: we have benchmark spreadsheets, e.g., for 2k concurrent short requests p95 ~180–240ms on dedicated clusters with kv caching and batching tuned. We'll share the raw CSVs.
[03:14] Sam: can we run a pilot where we run our prompt set and measure token/sec and p95?
[03:18] Maya: absolutely, we'll spin up a dedicated pilot — options: hosted trial for quick tests, or a temporary dedicated pool tied to your account. For strict KMS needs, private pilot is also possible but takes longer.
[03:29] Jenna: timeline wise we want POC next month, and decision in 6–8 weeks.
[03:33] Maya: that aligns well.
[03:35] [04:00] Diego: quick note on measurements: p95 is sensitive to seq len and concurrency. We'll instrument both first-token latency and completion latency and give token/sec numbers as tokens/s per GPU and overall cluster. We'll also include cold-starts if you plan to scale to zero.
[04:20] Sam: what's the impact of streaming on p95 and throughput?
[04:23] Diego: streaming requires more per-request overhead for chunking, but it lets clients render earlier tokens; throughput is slightly lower per-GPU due to more frequent push operations but you can batch streaming frames. In practice p95 for first byte tends to be lower than non-stream for interactive workflows.
[04:40] Tom: network topology — we need to keep traffic inside our VPC, can Redwood dedicated be deployed in our VPC?
[04:46] Maya: yes, our Private deployment supports customer VPC and on-prem. For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and private networking options but it's still managed by Redwood; if you need full control we recommend Private.
[04:58] Priya: and encryption? we want keys in our KMS and no plaintext logs outside our tenancy.
[05:03] Diego: for Private deployments we support customer KMS backing and logs can be routed to your logging endpoint; for Dedicated we can do bring-your-own-key for certain configurations. We'll clarify exact options in the security doc.
[05:15] Sam: any gotchas with batching and latency-sensitive workloads — we don't want batching to increase tail latency.
[05:21] Diego: good point — batching must be workload-aware. Redwood Optimize can suggest batch size and timeout configurations; and we have automatic dynamic batching that keeps batch windows low for interactive workloads while still improving throughput. Can also set strict SLOs to limit batching windows.
[05:36] Jenna: for our UI we stream partial completions at ~20 tokens increments, is that reasonable?
[05:41] Diego: yes 20-token frames are common; the runtime can flush every N tokens or after timeout. We'll test with your client and see best trade-off.
[05:48] Tom: curious about fallbacks — if a dedicated node is under pressure, can traffic failover to hosted with no changes?
[05:54] Maya: yes, smart routing supports policy-based fallback to hosted models or lower-cost variants. You can pin model versions and define fallback routes. There is some network routing config required but it's seamless at the API layer.
[06:05] Sam: how fast could we run a benchmark? we can provide prompt set and test account.
[06:09] Maya: if we start today we can provision a pilot cluster in ~3–5 business days for dedicated. Hosted trial is immediate. Private pilot takes 2–3 weeks.
[06:18] Priya: what about cost signals — if we need reserved capacity is there pricing for a small pilot?
[06:22] Maya: yes, we offer short-term reserved pilot pricing for 2–4 week dedicated pilots to validate performance; we'll include cost estimates in the follow-up.
[06:30] [06:45] Diego: just to capture technicals — your target p95 <=200ms for 50–150 tokens, concurrency ~300 peak, streaming required, token/sec target 1.5k across cluster. We'll design the pilot to measure first-byte and completion p95, tokens/sec per GPU, and end-to-end.
[06:58] Sam: correct. Also want to test model variants — 7B quantized vs 13B semi-quant, to check quality vs latency.
[07:06] Diego: noted. We can run both and give the latency-quality tradeoffs.
[07:10] Jenna: are there any security questionnaires or compliance docs we need to fill out?
[07:13] Maya: yes we'll send our security pack (SOC2, ISO summaries, network architecture) and a Data Processing Addendum; for custom private setups we can provide network diagrams.
[07:22] Tom: competitor question — we evaluated MegaCloud AI and GigaServe; what are typical differentiators?
[07:27] Maya: Redwood focuses on production economics and predictable tail latency, plus unified tooling across hosted/dedicated/private. We also surface cost/latency tradeoffs in the Console and offer Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization.
[07:38] Sam: any limitations on model size for streaming?
[07:41] Diego: no strict limit, but larger models increase token/sec cost — streaming works with all sizes but you'll see latency increases with 13B+ models unless you use quantization and optimized kernels.
[07:52] Priya: do you support our SSO (Okta) and provisioning?
[07:55] Maya: yes SSO/SAML + RBAC supported. We'll include steps for SSO setup.
[07:59] Sam: perfect.
[08:01] [08:30] Diego: okay I'll note action items for the SE side — run initial benchmark with your prompt set, provide CV/CSV results, and tune batching and KV cache.
[08:40] Maya: and I'll follow up with pricing and security docs.
[08:44] Jenna: thanks, one more quick question — do you have any logs for token-level cost breakdown?
[08:49] Maya: yes Redwood Console has token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and per model. We'll show that in the next demo.
[08:57] Tom: thanks, this was super helpful.
[09:00] Maya: recap and next steps...
[09:02] Maya: (1) Send security pack + SOC2, network diagram — Maya (by 2026-05-07) (2) Provision pilot cluster (dedicated) and seed test account — Diego (provision in 3–5 business days) (3) Run benchmark with Aurora prompt set and share raw CSVs — Diego & Sam (initial results by 2026-05-12) (4) Pricing for dedicated pilot and 3-month reserved option — Maya (by 2026-05-08) (5) Schedule technical deep dive/demo of Console and tracing — Maya to send invite for next week.
[09:26] Priya: can you include network ACL requirements in the security pack?
[09:29] Maya: yes will include.
[09:31] Sam: thanks everyone.
[09:33] Tom: thanks.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker labels generic (Speaker 6), minor transcription errors (KV cash, Samuel instead of SAML), filler words retained.
summary: Discovery focused on p95 <=200ms for 50-150 tokens, 300 concurrency peak, streaming required, token/sec target 1.5k. Evaluated hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs; prioritized SOC2/KMS and VPC requirements. Agreed to run dedicated pilot and benchmarks; Redwood to send security docs and pricing.
